title: Vaccines and Herd Immunity
text: Herd immunity (or community immunity) occurs when a sufficient proportion of a population has become immune to an infection — through vaccination or prior infection — thereby reducing the likelihood of further spread. The threshold proportion required for herd immunity varies by disease: for measles it is about 95%, for polio about 80–85%, and for influenza about 33–44%. Vaccination campaigns that achieve herd immunity protect vulnerable individuals who cannot be vaccinated (due to age or immune disorders). Herd immunity was instrumental in the eradication of smallpox and the near-elimination of polio. Declining vaccination rates due to vaccine hesitancy have led to resurgences of measles in several countries.
